1.pericope_label: The days of her purifying: seven days for a son, and twice that for a daughter

schools.summary: Give the historical answer to the doubled term, that the ancients believed the derangement of the system far greater at the birth of a girl, and show the belief was not peculiar to this law: the Greeks held that a man who had been near a woman in childbirth defiled the altar, one measure for purifying an island in their great war was to forbid women to be confined there, the Hindoos count a newborn's relations impure, and among the Arabs the mother remains unclean forty days. Notice too what the law omits, since it legislates only for ordinary cases and passes over twins, so the administrators under the second Temple had to supplement it, ruling that a mother of twins of both sexes kept the longer term.

Say the ceremony reminded the Jews of the common corruption of our nature, since the whole race of Adam is polluted, so the woman contracts uncleanness from the offspring she bears and is further contaminated by giving it birth; hence it appears how foul our condition is in God's sight, since at our birth, and before it, we infect our mothers. Correct what is an almost universal but very absurd reading, that what is condemned is libidinous intercourse, since the purification is not required unless there be offspring, so the impurity charged is not in the intercourse but in the generation. From this refute Pelagius, who denied that Adam's sin was propagated among his descendants and held that we contract sin by imitation and not by origin: the mother would not be unclean if the children were pure. Then guard marriage from the inference: if the marriage couch is free from stain that is due to God's indulgence, its sanctity covering what might otherwise be imputed as blame. On the doubled term for a daughter, canvass four answers before choosing. Some ascribe it to a natural cause; grant that continence was part of the intention but say the ceremony's object was different. Report the view that the mother is more defiled by female offspring because that sex is more disposed to vice, and say you know not whether it is sound. Think it more probable, as some hold, that the woman was the beginning of the rebellion, being deceived by the serpent and drawing husband and posterity into the same ruin. But hold it more correct that the punishment for males was lightened by circumcision, since although God consecrated both sexes in that symbol he honoured males by engraving his covenant on their flesh. Alongside this, make the eighth day depend on the mother, whose stricter period of uncleanness ends then.

Give a physical reason for the eighth day, that before this the child could scarcely have strength to bear the operation, and after it there was no need to delay, since until the rite was performed the child was not reckoned in covenant with God.

Reach the same doctrine by a shorter road, that this uncleanness signified the pollution of sin we are all conceived and born in, for if the root be impure so is the branch; and the mother's exclusion from the sanctuary signified that our original corruption would have shut us out for ever from God had he not provided for our purifying. On the doubled term, refuse to guess: why it should be double for a female you can assign no reason but the will of the Law-maker, adding that in Christ Jesus no difference is made of male and female. On the eighth day, note that the males shared the mother's pollution during the days of separation.

debates.question: Why is the term of purification doubled for a daughter?

sides.position: Because the punishment for males was lightened by circumcision, God having honoured them by engraving his covenant on their flesh — three other reasons being canvassed and found weaker
No reason can be assigned but the will of the Law-maker, and in Christ Jesus no difference is made of male and female
Because the ancients believed the physical derangement far greater at a girl's birth, a belief shared by Greeks, Hindoos and Arabs alike

debates.question: Why was circumcision fixed on the eighth day?

sides.position: Because the mother's stricter uncleanness ends then, and she no longer imparts defilement by touch
Because before then the child could scarcely bear the operation, and after it there was no reason to delay a rite that brought him into covenant

outliers.note: Alone turns the law into a refutation of Pelagius by name, arguing that the mother would not be unclean if the children were pure, so that sin is contracted by origin and not by imitation.

Alone shows the law's presuppositions were shared outside Israel, citing the Greek rule that a man near a woman in childbirth defiled the altar and the purifying of an island by forbidding confinements there.
Alone declines to explain the doubled term at all, assigning no reason but the will of the Law-maker and appealing to the abolition of the distinction in Christ.

themes: And the Lord spake unto Moses, saying,

Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, If a woman have conceived seed, and born a man child: then she shall be unclean seven days; according to the days of the separation for her infirmity shall she be unclean.
And in the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.
And she shall then continue in the blood of her purifying three and thirty days; she shall touch no hallowed thing, nor come into the sanctuary, until the days of her purifying be fulfilled.
But if she bear a maid child, then she shall be unclean two weeks, as in her separation: and she shall continue in the blood of her purifying threescore and six days.

6.pericope_label: A lamb for a burnt offering; and if she be not able to bring a lamb, two turtles

schools.summary: Insist that the purification was for the woman herself and not for the child, since it was the woman who was unclean and not the infant she had borne, the phrase meaning with regard to a son or a daughter according to which she had given birth. Fix the day as the forty-first or the eighty-first rather than the fortieth or the eightieth. Explain the inverted order of the two victims, that precedence goes to whichever is the costlier. Report from the ancients that the one gift confessed reproachful thoughts harboured before the birth and the other expiated words heedlessly spoken in the hour of anguish. And on the indulgence to the poor, add that the pair must be of one kind and not one of each, and that this was what the mother of our Lord presented at the Temple.

Give the ancient rule for the day, that a new mother waits until her sun is set and brings her offering on the morrow, the forty-first for a male and the eighty-first for a female. Report the rule of order as a Jewish commentator gives it, that in oblations the sacrifice for sin goes first, guilt being expiated so that the gift may be accepted, and confess that here the order is inverted and the reason not very apparent. From the poor woman's gift draw the state of poverty the mother of our Lord was in, and take her circumcising of the child and her purification together as showing that both were under the law and obedient to it.

Pause before the offerings to reject two explanations of the doubled term: there is probably no physical reason for the difference and it is difficult to assign a political one. Some of the ancient physicians assert that a woman is much longer recovering after the birth of a female, and answer that this is justified neither by observation nor by matter of fact; others think the difference intended to mark the inferiority of the female sex, which is a miserable reason, pitifully supported. On the poor woman's gift, turn it into an exclamation: the only heir to the throne of David was not able to bring a lamb to offer in sacrifice to God, and how abominable must sin be when it required him who was in the form of God thus to empty himself.

Take the first gift as thankfulness for a safe deliverance and hope of further favour to mother and child, since where there is joy there must be thanks and where there is hope there must be prayer; and note that the expiatory victim was identical for rich and poor, for whatever difference of means appears in the gifts of acknowledgment, the price of atonement is one. Allow two accounts of what it covered: the completing of a ceremonial defilement that merely figured moral pollution, or a real fault, whether an inordinate longing after children or impatience under the pangs of travail. Then press the poverty of Christ's parents, who could not bring a lamb, and that he was so early made under the law in order to redeem those that were under it.

debates.question: Why is the burnt offering named before the sin offering, against the usual order?

sides.position: The reason is not very apparent — the rule is that the sacrifice for sin goes first, guilt being expiated so that the gift may be accepted
Precedence goes to whichever victim is the costlier

debates.question: What was the sin offering for, when childbirth is no sin?

sides.position: Either to complete a ceremonial defilement that merely figured moral pollution, or to atone for a real fault — an inordinate longing after children, or impatience under the pangs of travail
To expiate words heedlessly spoken in the hour of anguish, the other gift confessing reproachful thoughts harboured before the birth

outliers.note: Alone comes back to the doubled term in order to demolish two explanations of it, calling the physicians' claim unsupported by observation and the appeal to female inferiority a miserable reason, pitifully supported.
Alone presses that the rite purified the woman and not the infant, since it was she who was unclean and the child was not.
Alone adds the practical rule that the two birds must be of one kind and not one of each, and locates the later ceremony at the eastern gate of the second Temple.

themes: And when the days of her purifying are fulfilled, for a son, or for a daughter, she shall bring a lamb of the first year for a burnt offering, and a young pigeon, or a turtledove, for a sin offering, unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, unto the priest:
Who shall offer it before the Lord, and make an atonement for her; and she shall be cleansed from the issue of her blood. This is the law for her that hath born a male or a female.

And if she be not able to bring a lamb, then she shall bring two turtles, or two young pigeons; the one for the burnt offering, and the other for a sin offering: and the priest shall make an atonement for her, and she shall be clean.
